intro: The Gayatri Mantra is one of the oldest and most widely recited verses in Hindu worship, found in the Rigveda (3.62.10) and traditionally attributed to the sage Vishvamitra. It is addressed to Savitr, the sun as the source of light and life, invoked here not as a distant deity but as the illuminator of the intellect. The verse is short - just four lines - built on the Vedic gayatri metre, from which it takes its popular name. It opens with the sacred syllable Om and the three vyahritis (bhuh, bhuvah, svah), moves to a description of the divine radiance of Savitr, and closes with a request that this radiance guide one's thinking. Across centuries it has been used in daily prayer, in the sandhyavandanam rites performed at dawn and dusk, and in the upanayana ceremony, where it is formally taught to a young student for the first time.

groups.heading: Om and the three worlds
groups.body: The opening line is Om bhur bhuvah svah. Om is treated in the Vedic and later tradition as the primordial sound, the root from which speech and creation are said to arise. The three words that follow - bhuh, bhuvah, svah - are the vyahritis, traditionally understood as naming the earthly realm, the intermediate or atmospheric realm, and the heavenly or luminous realm. Reciting them together at the start of the mantra is a way of situating the person praying within the whole of existence before the actual request is made. It functions as an invocation, gathering attention and settling the mind, rather than as a statement with a translatable meaning on its own.

groups.heading: Addressing Savitr
groups.body: The second line names the one being addressed: tat savituh varenyam, meaning roughly 'that excellent, desirable one, Savitr'. Savitr is a Vedic solar deity associated specifically with the sun at the moments of rising and setting, and more broadly with impelling or setting things in motion. Here the sun is approached not for warmth or harvest but as something worth turning toward, something chosen deliberately. This line sets up the rest of the Gayatri Mantra as an address to a particular form of light rather than a general statement about brightness.

groups.heading: The radiance that is sought
groups.body: The third line, bhargo devasya dhimahi, asks that the worshipper may meditate upon or hold in mind the bhargah - the radiance or splendour - of this god. The word dhimahi, 'we meditate', marks a shift from naming the deity to actively turning the mind toward that deity's quality. It is this line that gives the Gayatri Mantra its contemplative character: the request is not for an object or an event, but for sustained attention to a particular quality of light, understood in the tradition as linked to clarity of perception and understanding.

groups.heading: The request that completes the verse
groups.body: The final line, dhiyo yo nah prachodayat, is usually rendered as 'may that one inspire or direct our intellects'. This is the only line in the Gayatri Mantra that is phrased as a direct request, and it asks specifically for guidance of the buddhi, the faculty of discernment and understanding, rather than for any material outcome. Commentators across different periods have read this as the verse's central purpose: everything before it - the invocation of Om, the naming of the three worlds, the address to Savitr, the meditation on radiance - leads up to this one plea for a clearer, better-directed mind.

groups.heading: The verse as a whole
groups.body: Put together, the four lines of the Gayatri Mantra move from invocation to address to meditation to request. This structure is one reason the verse has been treated for so long as a self-contained unit of prayer rather than part of a longer hymn, even though it originates as a single verse within a larger Rigvedic hymn to Savitr. Its brevity and its grammatical completeness - it can be recited on its own and still make full sense - are part of why it has travelled so widely across different regions, lineages and daily practices over time.

groups.heading: Why it is called 'Gayatri'
groups.body: The name Gayatri Mantra does not refer to a deity but to the metre in which the verse is composed - gayatri chandas, a Vedic metre of three lines of eight syllables each. Several Vedic verses are composed in this metre, but this particular one, addressed to Savitr, came to be so closely identified with the metre itself that the two names are now used almost interchangeably in common speech. The personification of Gayatri as a goddess in later devotional literature is a separate development that grew up around the verse over time.

recitation: The Gayatri Mantra is traditionally recited during sandhyavandanam, the prayer performed at the junctions of the day - dawn, midday and dusk - particularly by those initiated through the upanayana ceremony, in which a teacher formally transmits the verse to a student for the first time. Many households also recite it as part of morning prayer, often facing the rising sun, sometimes accompanied by sipping water (achamana) and breath control (pranayama) as preparatory steps described in various ritual manuals. It is commonly repeated in multiples of three, nine, or 108 using a mala for counting, though the exact number varies by family custom and by the specific manual a household follows. Some recite it silently, some aloud; some precede it with the pranava Om and the vyahritis each time, as the text itself contains them, while others add further invocatory lines from their own regional tradition before beginning. It is also commonly recited at the start of other Vedic study or ritual, treated as an opening invocation suited to almost any occasion of learning or worship, rather than reserved for a single festival or date.
tradition: The tradition holds the Gayatri Mantra to be addressed to Savitr for the sake of clarity of mind, since its closing line is explicitly a request for the intellect to be rightly guided. Vedantic and ritual commentators over the centuries have described it as the mantra given to a student at the start of formal learning, which is why it remains central to the upanayana ceremony. Devotional literature from later periods personifies the verse as the goddess Gayatri and treats recitation as an act of reverence toward her as a form of the Divine Mother, though this is a layer added onto the original Rigvedic verse rather than part of it. Across these different readings, the consistent thread in how the tradition speaks of the Gayatri Mantra is its concern with inner clarity and right understanding, rather than with any specific worldly request.

faq.a: Gayatri is the name of the Vedic metre the verse is composed in - three lines of eight syllables each - not the name of a deity in the original Rigvedic text. The verse addressed to Savitr happens to be the best known example in this metre, which is why it is popularly called the Gayatri Mantra.

faq.q: Who is allowed to recite the Gayatri Mantra?
faq.a: Historically its recitation was tied to the upanayana ceremony and particular lineages, and practice has varied by community and period. Today it is widely recited across many households and backgrounds; anyone wanting to follow a particular restriction or custom is best guided by their own family or teacher's tradition.

faq.q: What is the meaning of the opening Om bhur bhuvah svah?
faq.a: Om is treated as the primordial sacred sound, and bhuh, bhuvah, svah are the three vyahritis, traditionally read as naming the earthly, atmospheric and heavenly realms. Together they form an invocation that opens the mind before the main request of the Gayatri Mantra is made.

faq.q: Is there a fixed number of times it should be chanted?
faq.a: Custom varies. Many recite it in sets of three, nine, or 108, often using a mala to keep count, but the specific number is a matter of family or lineage practice rather than a single rule given within the verse itself.

faq.q: Is the Gayatri Mantra only for the sun god?
faq.a: It is addressed specifically to Savitr, a Vedic deity associated with the sun's impelling, illuminating power, particularly at sunrise and sunset. Later devotional traditions also personify the verse as the goddess Gayatri, but the original request in the text is for guidance of the intellect, addressed to Savitr.
